items.prompt: Explain how sale and leaseback can weaken a business in a downturn.
items.canonical_answer: The business sells the asset, so what was an owned building becomes a lease payment. That payment falls due on fixed dates whatever revenue does. In a downturn revenue falls but the payment does not, so a larger share of shrinking cash goes to the lessor, and the business has lost the option it used to have of simply owning the premises and paying nothing for them. If the downturn is deep or long enough, the payment it cannot avoid is what turns a bad year into an unsurvivable one.

items.prompt: Evaluate whether a family-owned hotel that owns its building should use sale and leaseback to fund an extension.
items.canonical_answer: Probably not, unless no alternative exists. The decisive factor is that the hotel building is the family's main asset and the family intends to hold the business long term, so giving up ownership surrenders any future rise in the property's value permanently in exchange for a one-off sum. The strongest argument the other way is that the hotel needs a large amount now and a bank may not lend enough against a single property. The judgement would change if the extension is expected to raise annual profit by more than the lease payment and the family has no intention of selling the building anyway.

items.prompt: Evaluate whether the founders of a growing business should accept venture capital in exchange for a 30% stake.
items.canonical_answer: They should accept it, provided growth really is limited by capital they cannot raise elsewhere. That is the decisive criterion: if the business can reach its next stage on retained profit or borrowing, 30% is a very high price; if it cannot, 30% of a much larger business is worth more than 100% of a stalled one, and the investor's expertise and contacts add value beyond the money. The strongest argument against is the exit horizon rather than the stake itself - a venture investor expects to sell within a few years, so the founders are agreeing to run the business towards a sale on someone else's timetable, which rules out slow-payback strategies they might otherwise choose. The judgement reverses if the founders' plan pays off over a longer period than the investor will wait, or if a lender would fund the same growth against assets the business already has.
marking_guidance: A clear judgement is required, stated as a recommendation rather than as 'it depends'.
Context: the answer must turn on this business's position - whether capital is the binding constraint.
The decisive criterion must be named and explained.
The counterargument must be the strongest one, which is the exit horizon rather than dilution.
A condition under which the judgement reverses is required.

items.prompt: Evaluate whether a manufacturer should meet a temporary cash shortage with an overdraft or by delaying payment to suppliers.
items.canonical_answer: The overdraft is the better choice for a business that intends to keep trading with the same suppliers. The decisive factor is that delaying payment is not free: it costs supplier goodwill, may forfeit early-settlement discounts, and damages a credit standing that took years to build, whereas overdraft interest is a known, bounded cost. The strongest argument for delaying is that it costs no interest at all and requires nobody's permission. The judgement changes if the shortage is very short and small enough that a few days' delay would go unnoticed, or if the business has no overdraft facility and cannot obtain one quickly.

items.prompt: Explain why leasing costs more in total than buying the same asset outright.
items.canonical_answer: The lessor buys the asset and carries it on its own books, so it has money tied up in the asset for the whole term and it is the lessor, not the business, that bears the risk of the asset losing value. The lease payments have to cover the price of the asset, the cost to the lessor of having its money tied up, and a return for taking that risk. Added over a full term those payments therefore usually come to more than the purchase price. The business is paying for use and for the transfer of risk, not only for the asset - which is why the comparison is not simply 'leasing is a rip-off'.

Mechanism: payments must cover the price, the lessor's tied-up money and a return for risk.
Consequence: the total paid over a full term is usually more than the purchase price.
Must reach why the business may still choose it; do not accept the bare assertion that leasing costs more.

items.prompt: Evaluate whether a new delivery business should lease or buy its first three vehicles.
items.canonical_answer: Lease. items.prompt: Evaluate whether a business already carrying substantial debt should take a further bank loan to fund expansion.
items.canonical_answer: Usually not, without first changing something else. The decisive factor is that interest on existing debt already has to be paid whatever trading does, and adding more raises the fixed obligation the business must meet before it earns anything for its owners — which is most dangerous precisely when expansion does not deliver as planned. The answer changes if the expansion has predictable, contracted revenue attached, or if the business can fund part of it from retained earnings and borrow less.

items.prompt: Evaluate whether a growing business with a long cash cycle should use debt factoring.
items.canonical_answer: Yes, if growth is genuinely constrained by cash rather than by demand. The decisive factor is that the business is profitable on paper but cannot fund the next order, and factoring converts an existing asset into cash without adding debt or giving up ownership. The strongest argument against is the cost: the factor's percentage is charged on every invoice indefinitely, and customers dealing with a factor may read it as a sign of trouble. The business should also check whether the agreement is recourse or non-recourse, because under recourse it still carries the loss if a customer never pays, which removes one of the benefits it may think it is buying. The judgement changes if the business can instead shorten its own payment terms or negotiate longer terms from suppliers, which achieve the same effect at no cost.

items.prompt: A woman selling vegetables at a market wants to buy a refrigerated display unit. She has no collateral and no bank account history. Explain why micro-finance may be her only realistic source.

What any particular provider requires varies, so the point to make is that this is the route most likely to be open to her, not that it is certain. What it costs her is a higher interest rate than a bank would charge, and how much higher depends on the provider and on how micro-finance is regulated where she trades.

items.prompt: Explain why micro-finance interest rates are typically higher than commercial bank rates.
items.canonical_answer: Micro-finance lends to borrowers with no collateral and no credit history, so if a loan is not repaid the lender has nothing to recover, and the risk of that happening is higher than on secured commercial lending. The lender must cover those losses out of the interest it charges everyone else. Each loan is also small, so the work of assessing and collecting it is large relative to the sum lent. Both effects push the rate above commercial bank lending, and how far above depends on the provider and the market it operates in.

items.prompt: Evaluate the usefulness of micro-finance for developing enterprise in a rural economy.
items.canonical_answer: Useful, but for a specific purpose rather than as a route to growth. The decisive criterion is what the alternative actually is: for a borrower with no collateral and no credit history the realistic alternative is no finance at all, so a small expensive loan that starts a trading activity is worth more than a cheaper loan that is not available. In a rural economy that is the common case. The strongest argument against is the risk carried by the borrower: the rate is high, the sums are small, and a borrower whose venture fails still owes the money, with no limited liability to stand behind. The judgement changes as the enterprise grows - once a business has a record and something to pledge, micro-finance becomes the expensive option rather than the only one, and it cannot fund substantial expansion in any case.

items.prompt: Explain why a grant is often described as the cheapest external source of finance, and why that description can mislead.
items.canonical_answer: A grant is not repaid, so no capital leaves the business later; it carries no interest, so it creates no fixed obligation to meet in a poor year; and it gives away no ownership, so no share of future profit or control is surrendered. Borrowing costs interest; equity costs a share of ownership; asset finance costs both the use of the asset and a higher total price. A grant avoids all three at once, which is what the description is pointing at. The description misleads because avoiding those three costs is not the same as costing nothing: applying takes management time that could have been spent running the business, the conditions attached can push the business into choices it would not otherwise make, and internal sources also avoid all three while carrying costs of their own.

Mechanism: no repayment, no interest, no dilution - all three, which is what makes the description tempting.
Consequence: must reach the real costs - management time and conditions - not stop at 'it is free'.
Must reach the effect on the business: cheap is not the same as costless.

items.prompt: Evaluate whether a profitable family business should always exhaust internal sources before borrowing.
items.canonical_answer: No, not always. The decisive factor is the size and urgency of the need measured against what each internal source can actually release. items.prompt: Explain why equity finance places no burden on cash flow while debt finance does.
items.canonical_answer: Equity is not repaid and pays no interest. A dividend is discretionary: in a poor year the company can pay nothing, and the money stays in the business. Debt is contractual. Interest and instalments fall due on fixed dates regardless of trading, so in a poor year the payment must still be made out of reduced cash. The consequence is that the same fall in revenue leaves an equity-financed business with a smaller problem than a debt-financed one: one can hold its cash, the other must part with it at the worst moment. How large that difference is depends on how much debt is carried and how far revenue falls.

items.prompt: A profitable printing firm with a long trading record needs finance for a machine it expects to use for eight years. Its bank offers a five-year secured loan; an overdraft would cost less in interest over the first year. Evaluate the view that the firm should always choose the cheapest external source available.
items.canonical_answer: It should not, and this case shows why. The decisive criterion is suitability rather than price: the overdraft is cheaper over the first year but is repayable on demand, and the machine will take years to pay for itself, so the firm would be funding an eight-year asset with money the bank can withdraw at any point. The loan matches the life of the use. The strongest argument for the cheapest option is that cost is the one factor that can be measured with certainty in advance, while suitability is a judgement - and a firm that consistently pays more than it needs to will lose to competitors that do not. That argument holds where the two sources are genuinely interchangeable. It does not hold here, because they are not. The judgement would change if the machine were needed only for a short contract, or if the firm had cash coming in that would clear the overdraft within months.

items.prompt: Distinguish between the sources of finance available to a sole trader and those available to a public limited company.
items.canonical_answer: A sole trader cannot issue shares - an unincorporated business has none - so capital comes from the owner's own resources, retained profit, borrowing, trade credit and asset finance, and possibly a grant or crowd funding where the scheme allows. A public limited company may offer shares to the general public, which opens a source of equity no unincorporated form has. That legal difference is the decisive one. What follows from it is a tendency rather than a rule: the company is a separate borrower assessed on its own assets and record, and where it must file accounts there is verified information a lender can price - but limited liability protects the owners, not the lender, which is why a lender may still want security or personal guarantees from a small company.

items.prompt: Explain the matching principle and why breaking it damages a business.
items.canonical_answer: The matching principle holds that the life of a source should match the life of the use: long-term finance for non-current assets, short-term for working capital. items.prompt: KM Poultry is a private limited company with four years of trading and rising sales. It rents its sheds. It needs N$800 000 to add a processing line that will let it sell packaged portions rather than whole birds. The four shareholders are family and want to keep full ownership. Evaluate whether KM Poultry should finance the processing line with hire purchase.
items.canonical_answer: It should. Hire purchase is the source that fits KM Poultry's position, and the decisive factor is security. KM rents its sheds, so it has no property to pledge and an ordinary bank loan is unlikely to be offered on reasonable terms. Hire purchase is secured on the processing line itself, which removes that obstacle, and the instalments run over roughly the working life of the equipment, so the asset is paying for itself as it is paid for. It also leaves the family's ownership untouched, which they have said they want. The strongest viable alternative is an unsecured loan, since the family have ruled out new owners: it would leave the equipment unencumbered and might be arranged faster. It is the weaker option here because an unsecured lender has nothing to look to if KM cannot repay, so it will lend less and price the risk higher - and KM has no property to offer instead. The judgement would shift if a lender offered an unsecured loan at a materially lower total cost than the hire purchase, or if the family reconsidered outside ownership.

items.prompt: A tour operator earns 70% of its revenue in four months of the year and holds two months of operating cash in reserve. It is offered two options for the same amount: a five-year bank loan at a fixed rate repaid in equal monthly instalments, or an equity investment for 25% of the company. The equity is better where earnings are uncertain, because a shareholder absorbs a bad year and a lender does not, and where the investor brings expertise the business lacks. In a highly seasonal market the equity investment is the better choice. The decisive factor is that seasonal revenue arrives in concentrated periods while loan instalments fall due evenly through the year, so the business must hold cash through the lean months purely to service debt — cash that could otherwise fund stock for the peak. The recommendation would reverse if the lender agreed to structure repayments seasonally, which removes the mismatch and makes the cheaper option also the more suitable one.

items.prompt: Two businesses each need N$500 000: a six-year-old transport firm that owns its depot, and a start-up with an idea and no assets. Evaluate the claim that a bank loan is the best source of finance.
items.canonical_answer: The claim cannot be evaluated as stated, and that is the answer: a bank loan is right for the transport firm and wrong for the start-up, so 'best' is not a property a source can have on its own. The decisive criterion is the fit between what the source requires and what the business has. A bank generally wants security or a record before lending at an ordinary rate; the transport firm has both, so it is well placed for a predictable schedule without giving up ownership. The start-up has neither, so a loan is much less likely to be offered, and if it were the terms would reflect the whole risk sitting with the lender, and equity - which is paid for out of success rather than out of monthly cash - fits its position instead. The strongest argument for the claim is that a loan does suit the widest range of established businesses, so as a rule of thumb it is more often right than wrong. But a rule of thumb is not a judgement, and the same business changes: the start-up that survives three years and buys premises becomes exactly the business a loan suits.

items.prompt: A joinery business incorporated eight months ago, with no premises of its own, asks its bank for a loan. Explain why the bank may ask the two directors for personal guarantees.
items.canonical_answer: Because limited liability protects the directors, not the bank. Incorporation makes the company the borrower, so if this company cannot repay, the bank's claim is against the company's assets - and eight months old with no premises, it has very little to claim against, and no trading record for the bank to judge it on. The directors' own houses and savings are out of the bank's reach precisely because the business is incorporated. A personal guarantee puts them back within reach, which reduces what the bank stands to lose and is why it may be asked for here, where it might not be asked of a company with premises and eight years of accounts.
marking_guidance: Reason: limited liability restricts the directors' loss, not the bank's exposure.
Purpose: the guarantee restores the bank's claim against personal assets.
Context: the answer must use the age of the company and the absence of premises.
Do not accept the reverse claim that limited liability makes lending safer.
Conditional language expected - the bank may ask, and might not of an established company.

items.prompt: Explain the difference between an internal and an external source of finance.
items.canonical_answer: The difference is whether a party outside the business supplies the money. Internal finance comes from the business's own trading, its assets or its existing owners: retained earnings, selling an asset, cash released from working capital. External finance comes from someone outside: a lender, a new owner, a supplier granting credit, or a grant-giver. The consequence is that internal finance charges no interest and dilutes no ownership but is limited to what the business already has, while external finance can be far larger but brings an obligation to repay, or a new owner, or conditions attached.
marking_guidance: Both sides of the distinction are required.
Boundary: whether the money comes from outside the business is the line.
Reward a stated consequence of the difference, not only the difference itself.

items.provenance: Added 2026-09-08 under CR-003 to satisfy RS-37: the objective predicted this command word and carried no item shaped for it.
items.prompt: Explain one reason a large company might issue debentures rather than new shares.
items.canonical_answer: Because a debenture raises a large sum without giving anyone a share of ownership. The debenture holder is a lender, not an owner, so existing shareholders keep the same proportion of the company and the same control, and the cost is a known fixed rate of interest rather than an open-ended claim on future profits. The price of that is an obligation: the interest is due whether or not the company profits, and the sum must be repaid on the redemption date.
marking_guidance: Reason: ownership and control are not diluted.
Mechanism: the holder is a lender, so the cost is fixed interest rather than a share of profit.
Must state the corresponding obligation to earn full credit.

items.provenance: Added 2026-09-08 under CR-003 to satisfy RS-37: the objective predicted this command word and carried no item shaped for it.
items.prompt: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage to existing partners of admitting a new partner to raise finance.
items.canonical_answer: The advantage is that the capital carries no interest and need not be repaid, so it places no burden on the partnership's cash flow in a poor year, and a new partner often brings skills and contacts as well as money. The disadvantage is permanent: the new partner takes a share of future profits and a share of control, so decisions the existing partners could once take alone now need agreement.
marking_guidance: Both an advantage and a disadvantage are required.
Reason: no interest and no repayment on one side; a permanent share of profit and control on the other.
Reward the point that the cost is permanent while the capital is one-off.

items.provenance: Added 2026-09-08 under CR-003 to satisfy RS-37: the objective predicted this command word and carried no item shaped for it.
items.prompt: Explain why a business might choose hire purchase rather than paying cash for a vehicle.
items.canonical_answer: Because hire purchase spreads the cost over the period the vehicle is being used, so the business keeps its cash for trading rather than tying it up in one payment, and it still owns the vehicle once the final instalment is paid. The finance is secured on the vehicle itself, so a business with little else to pledge can still obtain it. The cost is that the total paid is higher than the cash price, and the vehicle can normally be repossessed if instalments are missed.
marking_guidance: Reason: the cost is spread over the period of use while ownership still passes at the end.
Mechanism: cash is retained for trading; the asset itself provides the security.
Must state the higher total cost or the repossession risk.

items.provenance: Added 2026-09-08 under CR-003 to satisfy RS-37: the objective predicted this command word and carried no item shaped for it.
items.prompt: Explain why a mortgage usually carries a lower interest rate than an unsecured loan of the same size.
items.canonical_answer: Because the loan is secured on property. If the business does not repay, the lender has a named asset to look to rather than nothing, so the loss it expects is smaller than on the same sum lent unsecured. What the lender may actually do to recover the property, and how long it takes, is set by national law and differs between countries. A lender prices for the loss it expects, so a smaller expected loss supports a lower rate, and the strength of the security is also why a mortgage can be very large and run for many years.
marking_guidance: Reason: the property gives the lender a way to recover the money.
Mechanism: a smaller expected loss supports a lower rate.
Reward the link between the strength of the security and the size and length of the loan.

items.provenance: Added 2026-09-08 under CR-003 to satisfy RS-37: the objective predicted this command word and carried no item shaped for it.
items.prompt: Explain why trade credit is described as interest-free finance, and why it is not free.
items.canonical_answer: It is described as interest-free because the supplier charges nothing for the delay: goods arrive now and are paid for in 30 or 60 days, and no interest appears anywhere. It is not free because something is usually given up for it. A supplier offering a discount for early settlement is charging the business that discount for taking the full period, and paying later than agreed costs the business its standing with the supplier and may cost it credit terms later.
marking_guidance: Reason: no interest is charged for the delay in payment.
Mechanism: the discount forgone, or the damage to supplier relations, is the real cost.
Both halves of the question must be answered.

items.prompt: A family bakery has traded for eight years and already repays two loans. It needs finance for a delivery van it will run for six years, and for a stock build before the festive season. Analyse two factors that should influence the sources it chooses.
items.canonical_answer: The use to which the money is put is the first. The van will be used for six years, so the finance for it should last about that long - hire purchase or a term loan - because a source repayable sooner would fall due while the van is still earning back its cost, forcing the bakery to find the money from trading or to sell an asset it needs. The stock build is the opposite: the money is needed for weeks, so short-term finance such as trade credit or an overdraft avoids paying for years of borrowing to solve a problem lasting one season. The level of existing debt is the second. Two loans are already being repaid, so further borrowing adds to a fixed obligation that must be met whatever the festive season brings; a lender assessing the bakery is likely to see more risk and price the new borrowing accordingly, or ask for more security. If the festive trade is as reliable as eight years of trading suggests, that risk is manageable; if it is not, the bakery would do better to fund the stock build from supplier credit than to add a third repayment.
marking_guidance: Two factors are required, each developed as a chain rather than named.
Condition: the differing lives of the two needs, and the debt already carried.
Mechanism: source life against use life; fixed obligations against variable seasonal revenue.
Consequence: must reach an effect on the bakery's objectives or its ability to trade.
Conditional language expected; do not credit a bare list of the five factors.
Objective or stakeholder: the chain must land on an effect the business or a stakeholder feels.

items.prompt: Explain one benefit and one drawback to a sole trader of financing expansion from her own savings.
items.canonical_answer: The benefit is that the money costs nothing to use and changes nothing about who owns the business: there is no interest, no repayment schedule and no outside party to satisfy, so a poor trading month creates no new obligation. The drawback is that it moves her personal wealth into a business that may fail, and because liability is unlimited her savings were already exposed - so the expansion increases how much of her own money is at risk on one outcome, and the amount she can raise is capped by what she happens to have.
marking_guidance: Reason: no interest, no repayment and no dilution on one side.
Purpose: the money is under the owner's own control and creates no obligation in a poor month.
Why the drawback matters: personal wealth is moved into a business that may fail, and the sum is capped.
Both halves of the question must be answered.

items.prompt: A delivery van has a cash price of N$150 000. On hire purchase the business pays a deposit of N$30 000 and 36 monthly instalments of N$4 200. Calculate the total amount paid and the extra cost over the cash price.
items.canonical_answer: Total paid = deposit + (instalments x amount) = N$30 000 + (36 x N$4 200) = N$30 000 + N$151 200 = N$181 200. Extra cost over the cash price = N$181 200 - N$150 000 = N$31 200. As a proportion of the cash price that is 31 200 / 150 000 = 20.8%, which is the price of spreading the payments over three years.
marking_guidance: Formula: total paid = deposit + (number of instalments x instalment).
Substitution must be shown, not only the answer.
Units: the currency must appear on every figure.
Interpretation: one sentence saying what the extra amount represents earns the final mark.

items.provenance: Added 2026-09-08 after review issue SR-9609-5.2-CODEX-R2-011 (RS-22, RS-37).
items.prompt: A business finds that buying a machine on hire purchase costs N$31 200 more than the N$150 000 cash price. It has N$160 000 in the bank. Interpret that figure for the decision it faces.
items.canonical_answer: The N$31 200 is 20.8% of the cash price - what the business pays for keeping its money for three years instead of handing it over now. Set against N$160 000 in the bank, paying cash would leave only N$10 000 of working capital, so the comparison is not simply 'cash is cheaper': it is whether N$31 200 is a reasonable price for keeping N$150 000 available for wages, stock and the unexpected. If the business would otherwise have to borrow that working capital at a higher rate, hire purchase is cheaper overall; if it has steady cash coming in and no other use for the money, it is not.
marking_guidance: Comparison: the figure must be set against the cash price or the cash the business holds, not read on its own.
Meaning: must interpret the extra cost as the price of retaining cash, not as a penalty.
Reward the point that the alternative use of the cash decides the answer.
